title: NHS Pension Scheme (CAS-118205-Z8C1)
text:
CAS-118205-Z8C1
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mrs S
Scheme NHS Pension Scheme (the Scheme)
Respondents NHS Business Services Authority (NHS BSA)
Sherwood Forest Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (the
Employer)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
1
NHS BSA, Sherwood Forest Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

CAS-118205-Z8C1
In 2011, NHS BSA sent Mrs S an NHS Pension Choice Statement. The information
was calculated on 6 April 2011 using details notified by her Employer up to 31 March
2010. The figures were calculated to show her benefits at age 55. The information
showed:-
• The Normal Pension Age (NPA) for the Scheme was 60, but as she was a
member of the special classes, she had the right to retire at age 55 with an
unreduced pension.
• Total membership was 24 years 341 days.
• Annual pension was £10,144.00.
• Lump sum was £30,433.00.
Or
• Maximum lump sum was £54,344.00.
• Reduced pension was £8,152.00.
On 23 February 2023, Mrs S telephoned NHS BSA to obtain an accurate pension
quotation ahead of her intended retirement age of 55, a few months later. She was
informed that she did not hold SCS as her capacity code had been changed by her
Employer. She was advised to contact her Employer who could rectify her capacity
code.
On the same day, Mrs S telephoned the Employer who was unable to rectify the
issue. She was advised to continue via NHS BSA’s Internal Dispute Resolution
Procedure (IDRP) to resolve the matter.
On 31 March 2023, Mrs S submitted her complaint under stage one of the Scheme’s
IDRP. She said:-
• She joined the NHS in 1990 as a Nursing Auxiliary and was granted SCS at that
time, allowing for retirement with an unreduced pension from age 55.
• She had worked continuously for the NHS since 1990, with no break in
pensionable employment, and her role changed in 2000 when she became an
ODP/Scrub Nurse, a role which had not changed since.
2

CAS-118205-Z8C1
• She repeatedly sought accurate pension forecasts from the Employer but was
unable to access her details through the Electronic Staff Record (ESR) system
until nearer her retirement age. It was only then that she discovered that her
retirement age was recorded as 60.
• She contacted NHS Pensions in February 2023 and was informed that her record
showed her as an “Officer”, which she considered to be incorrect given her
nursing background and previous SCS entitlement.
• The 2011 Choice Statement confirmed her SCS and entitlement to retire at 55,
and that she was never informed of any change to this when she became an ODP
in 2000.
• She disputed the Capacity Code change from 1 to 4 on 1 September 2012, stating
that she had no role change at that time and was not consulted or notified. The
administrative change caused the loss of her SCS.
• Her current role continues to involve direct patient care, constant attendance,
lifting, and administration of treatment and drugs - duties she says align with the
definition of “arduous” nursing work.
• She noted that other staff performing identical duties were classed as Anaesthetic
or Scrub Nurses and had retained SCS, so it was unfair and inconsistent for her to
have lost SCS.
• She cited NHSBSA v Williams (2017) ICR 327 and Royal College of Nursing
guidance as supporting her view that her role continued to qualify for SCS, given
its patient-facing and physically demanding nature.
On 5 July 2023, NHS BSA responded under stage one of the Scheme’s IDRP. It
said:-
• It acknowledged Mrs S’ concern that her ESR showed a retirement age of 60 and
that her capacity code no longer reflected nursing status. It confirmed that her last
employment attracting SCS ended on 31 January 2007.
• It explained that capacity codes were assigned by the Employer and that, under
Regulation R2(1)(a)(i) of the Regulations, only employment as a nurse,
physiotherapist, midwife or health visitor qualified for SCS.
• While it accepted that there may be overlap between the duties of an ODP and a
Theatre Nurse, it maintained that ODPs were regulated by the Health and Care
Professions Council (HCPC), not the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), and
therefore were not classed as nurses for the purposes of SCS.
• The Regulations had been correctly applied and that Mrs S did not attract SCS.
On 21 July 2023, Mrs S’ Employer contacted NHS BSA. It stated that in certain
circumstances an ODP could qualify for SCS. It had compared the job description for
3

CAS-118205-Z8C1
a Registered Nurse and ODP and saw no distinction. It requested that NHS BSA
confirm whether Mrs S’ SCS could be reinstated.
On 20 October 2023, Mrs S escalated her complaint under stage two of the Scheme’s
IDRP. She said:-
• The Employer conducted its own internal investigation and supported her position
that she continued to hold SCS. However, NHS BSA had not engaged with the
evidence and simply reiterated its position without further analysis.
• She highlighted that her contract of employment identified her as a “Clinical Nurse
Grade C (Whitley Grade)”, under the Nurses and Midwives Whitley Council Terms
and Conditions, confirming continuous service from 5 November 1990 and
therefore eligibility for SCS.
• Her role and duties remained nursing in nature, despite her ODP qualifications,
and she had always worked under nursing regulations, pay scales, and
contractual terms.
• She stated that a Band 5 HCPC-registered Physiotherapist attracted SCS and
questioned why an ODP holding HCPC registration and performing nursing duties
was treated differently.
• She reiterated that her 2011 Choice Statement confirmed SCS entitlement and
that she never received any notice of a change. She questioned how NHS BSA
could issue such documentation four years after claiming her SCS ended in 2007,
without later notification of amendment.
• She argued that NHS BSA’s handling was procedurally inconsistent, particularly
as it initially stated that capacity codes were Employer-controlled but had since
disregarded the Employer’s confirmation of her nursing status.
• She had suffered financial, physical, and emotional hardship as a result of the
ongoing delay, noting she planned to retire at 55 in line with SCS and that her
husband had already retired. She asked that the case be treated as urgent and
her SCS reinstated. She cited another former Auxiliary Nurse to ODP colleague
who retired at 55 on SCS terms at a neighbouring NHS Trust.
On 14 December 2023, NHS BSA responded under stage two of the Scheme’s IDRP.
It said:-
• Mrs S correctly held SCS from 1990 as a consequence of her role as a Nursing
Assistant. This would have continued while she remained in that role, or as a
Health Care Assistant, under the same employment contract.
• Once Mrs S moved from her original role, to an ODP, the Employer should have
updated her Capacity Code to reflect the new job title, and she should no longer
have been recorded as a Nurse. It also explained that historic SCS could have
resumed if she had later entered another qualifying nursing post.
4

CAS-118205-Z8C1
• The reference to Nurse Grade C in Mrs S’ contract related only to the pay scale
used for ODPs. It did not indicate that she was a registered nurse or employed in
a nursing capacity.
• It accepted that ODPs carried out clinical duties and that some tasks may have
overlapped with those performed by Theatre Nurses. However, such overlaps also
existed between other clinical professions and did not, on their own, meet the
requirement of being employed as a Nurse.
• The ODP and nursing professions were distinct, with different qualifications,
responsibilities and regulatory bodies. Mrs S’ job description clearly differentiated
her duties from those of registered nurses.
• ODPs were not included in the list of professions eligible for SCS under the
Regulations. Carrying out some duties similar to nurses did not create eligibility
where the role itself was not a nursing role.
Mrs S’ position
She was never notified of any withdrawal of SCS and that the 2011 Choice Statement
confirmed her entitlement at age 55.
The Regulations had been misapplied, and NHS BSA had relied on job titles and
registration bodies rather than the substance of her role. She said the approach was
inconsistent with the Ombudsman’s previous decisions.
She submitted that her duties were indistinguishable from those of Theatre Nurses
and Midwives, noting that she works identical shifts, attended the same mandatory
courses, and provides clinical care in obstetrics, theatres, wards, and emergency
settings. Therefore, her exclusion from SCS was unjust and discriminatory.
She stated that the NHS BSA’s administrative failings, including delays, inconsistent
explanations, and lack of notice regarding pension changes, had caused financial,
physical, and emotional distress, particularly as she was due to retire in June 2023
and remained in full-time work despite ill health.
5

CAS-118205-Z8C1
NHS BSA’s position
NHS BSA chose to rely on the arguments conveyed in its stage one and two IDRP.
The Employer’s position
It had contacted NHS BSA to confirm whether Mrs S’ capacity code could be returned
to 1 so that her SCS could be reinstated.
Based on the accessible guidance, it understood that Mrs S was not eligible but had
been awaiting confirmation from NHS BSA.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
The question of Mrs S’ entitlement to SCS was whether her current employment can
properly be regarded as “pensionable employment as a nurse” under Regulation R2.
That term was not expressly defined in the Regulations, so it had to be interpreted in
line with its ordinary meaning, aided by any relevant case law. The High Court’s
judgment in NHS BSA v Williams [2017] ICR 327 (Williams) is particularly instructive
on this point. In Williams, Warren J held that “employment as a nurse” in the context
of the Regulations was intended to capture principally those members of the Scheme
“who were qualified Nurses employed in a nursing job”.
The court made clear in Williams that it was not sufficient to look only at the nature of
a person’s duties; it was also necessary to consider their job title, job description, and
importantly their qualifications. In other words, one cannot qualify as being “employed
as a nurse” purely by performing nursing-type tasks. The role had to be substantively
a nursing post held by a suitably qualified nurse. Warren J went on to note that a
nursing qualification is “part and parcel of being in pensionable employment as a
nurse”, just as much as it was for the other SCS categories which all require specific
professional qualifications.
He cautioned against focusing exclusively on job function to the exclusion of formal
role criteria, stating that “it would be wrong […] to ignore the job title and job
descriptions and qualifications of the person concerned and to focus exclusively on
job function”. Furthermore, the judgment stated plainly that “if a person cannot be
described as a Nurse in the first place, that person cannot be in pensionable
employment as a Nurse.” Adopting the precedent set by that case was in line with
previous Ombudsman’s decisions.
Mrs S’ job title and professional registration were those of an ODP, not a Nurse. For
example, the person specification for a Band 5 Theatre Nurse would have required a
valid NMC nursing registration, whereas Mrs S’ ODP post could have been, and was,
undertaken with an HCPC registration instead.
6

CAS-118205-Z8C1
The NHS job description for a Senior ODP explicitly allowed for alternative titles such
as “Deputy Sister/Charge Nurse/Senior Operating Department Practitioner” which
indicated that the role might have equally been filled by a nurse or by an ODP. Mrs S,
however, was appointed in the ODP capacity. The evidence showed she was able to
fully perform the duties of her position as a Senior ODP without holding an NMC
nursing qualification. The fact that her day-to-day clinical tasks in theatre may have
been very similar to those of an NMC-registered Theatre Nurse did not mean she was
employed as a nurse.
As per Williams, a line had to be drawn between what constitutes supporting nursing
duties and what constitutes being a nurse in the eyes of the Regulations. Mrs S’ role
fell on the wrong side of that line. She could not be described as a nurse because of
her specific qualification and official role.
It was important to clarify where Mrs S’ case differed to the type of case which may
have previously been upheld, for example, in a previous Ombudsman decision CAS-
37294-G0Y2. In that case, the definition of “Nurse” for SCS purposes was examined
in a scenario where a member had moved through different NHS roles. The member
had held posts which did require a nursing qualification, and the issue was whether
she retained SCS upon moving into certain managerial positions.
By contrast, Mrs S’ post-2000 employment had been in a role that did not require a
nursing qualification. Unlike the applicant in CAS-37294-G0Y2, Mrs S could not
perform a role for which holding an NMC registration was an essential requirement.
For example, she would not have been eligible for a position as a “Theatre Nurse” or
“Clinical Nurse Specialist” unless she held a nursing qualification, which she does
not. Her HCPC registration allowed her to work as an ODP, but it was not equivalent
to being a registered nurse in the context of the Regulatory criteria.
The Adjudicator also considered the supportive statements from Mrs S’ Employer
which suggested that her role remained “nursing in nature” and on former Whitley
Council nursing terms. However, the Employer’s characterisation, while well-
intentioned, could not override the objective requirements of the Scheme
Regulations. The Regulations themselves did not include ODPs in the cohort of staff
eligible for SCS and it was ultimately the Regulations, as interpreted by the courts,
which determined entitlement, not internal NHS job classification, or terminology.
Mrs S had also argued that her contract of employment confirmed her title as Clinical
Nurse Grade C. The Adjudicator reviewed the contract of employment and
considered Mrs S’ observation to be factually incorrect.
While the job advert and job description advertised the role as a Registered
Nurse/ODP, those documents were generic and not specific to Mrs S. The only
document specific to and signed by Mrs S was the Contract of Employment which
specifically stated her title was an ODP and only an ODP. The “Whitley Grade”
grading system used internally by the Employer did not confer rights or
7

CAS-118205-Z8C1
responsibilities outside of those inherent to the role of an ODP. For the purposes of
SCS, Mrs S’ role was an ODP not a nurse.
Given that Mrs S was a member of the Scheme before SCS was abolished in 1995, it
was understandable that she expected to retain that status, and it was acknowledged
why she felt aggrieved when informed that she did not. Mrs S’ point that she was
employed as a Nursing Auxiliary since 5 November 1990, which, on occasion, had
been granted SCS, when undertaken alongside holding a Nursing Qualification was
noted.
It was noted that the Employer requested the reinstatement of her SCS which NHS
BSA have declined. While the Employer’s acknowledgment of its error was noted, the
ultimate decision whether to award unreduced retirement rests with NHS BSA.
Despite any expectations that may have arisen from the Employer’s failure to update
Mrs S’ employee information, Mrs S’ role as an ODP still did not attract SCS. NHS
BSA are bound by the Regulations and were not permitted to contradict them, even
where the Employer had misrepresented Mrs S’ eligibility. It had to pay members the
benefit to which they were entitled.
The Adjudicator also considered whether any poor conduct from NHS BSA or the
Employer, for example the provision of incorrect information, constituted non-financial
8

CAS-118205-Z8C1
injustice. It was noted that, even where it is recognised that incorrect information had
been provided, this did not always result in a payment for non-financial injustice.
It was accepted that Mrs S received a pension forecast in 2011 which confirmed an
NRA of 55. It was likely that forecast was produced on the basis of outdated
employment information held on NHS BSA’s database, which had not yet been
amended to reflect her 2000 transfer from a Nursing Auxiliary post (which attracted
SCS) to an ODP post (which did not). The subsequent update to her Capacity Code
in 2012 corrected that error. It was the Employer’s responsibility to provide NHS BSA
with up-to-date, accurate employee information. As it failed to uphold that
responsibility, notice or rectify the issue for over 10 years, it was a considerable
administrative failure.
Page 8-9 of the NHS Pension Special Class Status Employer Factsheet states, “If SC
status ceases due to a change in duties, or if it is removed due to a correction to
employment records, Employers must also inform the member.” There was no
evidence of Mrs S’ Employer upholding this requirement.
Mrs S also stated that she had not seen a pension forecast until near her intended
retirement date of 55 because she was unable to view her ESR. The review to her
eligibility took place in 2012 at which point her record was amended to reflect her
appropriate retirement age of 60. It was unclear how and why Mrs S was unable to
access her ESR but from the documentary evidence available, it appeared Mrs S did
not receive, or access retirement estimates from 2011 until near her intended
retirement date. Given that the 2011 choice statement provided greatly outdated
information, and that information was an estimate, it would have been prudent to
resolve the ESR issue prior to making any financial decisions.
9

CAS-118205-Z8C1
• She disagreed with the Adjudicator's finding that she could have remained in
Theatres as an Auxiliary Nurse without obtaining an ODP qualification and would
have been eligible for SCS in that capacity. She submitted that obtaining an
additional qualification should not have caused the loss of an entitlement she
would otherwise have retained.
• An email dated 7 July 2023 from an SFH Pensions Supervisor, which she said
confirmed that other NHS Trusts had ODPs who did in fact qualify for SCS. She
argued this supported her position that the system was being applied
inconsistently.
• There had been maladministration by NHS BSA, not only by the Employer,
pointing to the fact that NHS BSA issued a pension forecast in 2011 confirming
SCS and a retirement age of 55, four years after claiming her SCS had ended in
January 2007.
• She said the Employer's errors had directly prevented her from retiring as
planned, caused significant financial hardship, and that her husband had been
forced to return to work following his own retirement after the expected pension
lump sum did not materialise.
• She disputed that she bore any responsibility for failing to obtain further pension
forecasts, given that the forecasts she had received had consistently confirmed
SCS entitlement, and that colleagues in the same position had retired at 55
without issue.
• She submitted that the £500 injustice award did not adequately reflect the
sustained and serious impact on her health, finances, and personal life over a
period of more than 30 years of NHS service.
• Under the Regulations, she could have reverted to an Auxiliary Nurse role five
years prior to her intended retirement and thereby retained SCS. She was never
afforded that opportunity due to the ongoing misinformation she received.
51. I have considered the additional points made by Mrs S, but they do not change the
outcome. I agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
52. Mrs S has complained that NHS BSA denied her the right to retire at age 55 on an
unreduced pension under SCS, on the basis that her role as an ODP is not
"pensionable employment as a nurse" within the meaning of Regulation R2. She has
said that her duties as an ODP are identical to those of a nurse.
53. The question of Mrs S' entitlement to SCS is whether her employment can properly
be regarded as "pensionable employment as a nurse" under Regulation R2. That
term is not expressly defined in the Regulations, so it must be interpreted in line with
its ordinary meaning, aided by relevant case law. The High Court's judgment in NHS
10

CAS-118205-Z8C1
BSA v Williams [2017] ICR 327 (Williams) is particularly instructive on this point. In
Williams, Warren J held that "employment as a nurse" in the context of the
Regulations was intended to capture principally those members of the Scheme "who
were qualified Nurses employed in a nursing job."
54. The court made clear in Williams that it is not sufficient to look only at the nature of a
person's duties; it is also necessary to consider their job title, job description, and,
importantly, their qualifications.
55. This approach is exemplified by the recent Determination in CAS-77785-QSH0, in
which the complaint was upheld on the basis that the applicant's employment as a
Theatre Team Leader qualified as "pensionable employment as a nurse" under
Regulation R2. In that case, the applicant was a Registered General Nurse (RGN)
who had maintained continuous registration with the NMC throughout her
employment. Although the person specification for the Theatre Team Leader role
permitted either RGN or ODP registration, I found that the applicant had qualified for
and filled the role by virtue of her nursing qualification and was therefore "a qualified
nurse employed in a nursing job." Critically, the role required a healthcare
qualification but as the applicant occupied the role in the capacity of a nurse, she met
that requirement as a nurse. It followed that she was employed as a nurse for the
purposes of Regulation R2.
56. The above case contrasts with another recent Determination in CAS-58918-R9V9
which is more similar to Mrs S' situation. On the basis that qualification, job title and
job function are all required to be taken into account in determining whether a person
is "in pensionable employment as a nurse" for the purpose of Regulation R2, I
concluded in that case that Mr E was not employed as a nurse but instead was
employed as an ODP. This is notwithstanding that his role was a role that could also
have been filled by a person qualified and registered as a nurse and that the job
description allowed alternative job titles as "Deputy Sister/ Charge Nurse/Senior
Operating Department Practitioner" and could have been filled by either a person
qualified as a nurse or as an ODP. Mr E was not registered as a nurse but as an ODP
and was able to fulfil his role as a Senior ODP. The fact that his job functions would
have been no different if he had been registered as a nurse and employed as such
rather than as an ODP does not mean that he was in "employment as a nurse".
57. The position in the present case is the same as CAS-58918-R9V9 and the inverse of
CAS-77785-Q5H0. Mrs S does not hold an NMC nursing registration. Her
professional registration is with the HCPC as an ODP. She is therefore not a person
who can be described as a nurse in the first place. Applying the reasoning in Williams
and following the approach taken in CAS-77785-QSH0 and CAS-58918-R9V9, it
follows that Mrs S cannot be in pensionable employment as a nurse for the purposes
of Regulation R2, regardless of the clinical duties she performs day to day.
58. The distinction between the two cases is a fundamental one. In CAS-77785-QSH0,
the applicant's qualification and professional registration were those of a nurse, and
the role she occupied required a nursing or equivalent healthcare qualification. She
11

CAS-118205-Z8C1
Mrs S has submitted that, had she been aware of her position, she could have
reverted to an Auxiliary Nurse role in the five years prior to her intended retirement
and thereby retained SCS, and that she was denied that opportunity by the
misinformation she received. I accept that, had she reverted to a qualifying Auxiliary
Nurse role within the requisite five-year period prior to retirement, she would indeed
12

CAS-118205-Z8C1
have retained SCS. However, I do not consider that the full weight of responsibility for
this missed opportunity can be attributed to NHS BSA.
The 2011 benefit statement, whilst initially inaccurate, was corrected to accurately
reflect Mrs S' position in 2012. From that point, the information necessary for Mrs S to
understand that she no longer held SCS was readily available to her. Had she
reviewed her choice statement or any of her annual benefit statements at any point
after 2012, she would have seen that her normal retirement age was recorded as 60
rather than 55, which I would consider a reasonably obvious change to notice, even
on a cursory review. Given that Mrs S wished to retire in 2023, the latest she could
have reverted to an Auxiliary Nurse role and still satisfied the five-year qualifying
period was 2018. She therefore had approximately six years, between 2012 and
2018, during which she could have identified the change in her retirement age from
her benefit statements and taken steps accordingly.
Whilst I acknowledge that the failure to notify Mrs S when her capacity code was
amended in 2012 amounts to maladministration, it cannot be said that NHS BSA
bears sole responsibility for Mrs S' position when the information she needed to
protect her interest was accessible to her throughout that period.
Therefore, I uphold Mrs S’ complaint in part.
Directions
With 28 days of the date of this Determination, the Employer shall:-
• Pay Mrs S £500 in recognition of the distress and inconvenience she has
experienced.
13

CAS-118205-Z8C1
Camilla Barry
Deputy Pensions Ombudsman
15 July 2026

Appendix One
Extract from NHS Pension Scheme Regulations 1995 (as amended) SI 1995/300
“Nurses, physiotherapists, midwives and health visitors
R2.—(1) Subject to paragraph (2), this regulation applies to a member—
(a) who, at the coming into force of these Regulations—
(i) is in pensionable employment as a nurse, physiotherapist, midwife or health
visitor, or
(ii) has accrued rights to benefits under the scheme arising out of a previous
period in which she was engaged in such employment and at no time since the
last occasion on which she was so engaged has she had a break in
pensionable employment for any one period of 5 years or more,
and
(b) who spends the whole of the last 5 years of her pensionable employment as a
nurse, physiotherapist, midwife or health visitor.
(2) This regulation shall cease to apply if the member has a break in pensionable
employment for any one period of 5 years or more ending after the coming into force of
these Regulations.
(3) Where this regulation applies—
(a) regulation E1 (normal retirement pension) will apply to the member as if the
reference, in paragraph (1) of that regulation, to age 60, were a reference to age
55;”
